Hey everyone, how are you? I'm Danny Kawarzazki, professional wheelchair tennis player from Spain and I also co-founded a marketing agency specialized in the professionalization of Olympic sports and the normalization of disability through media. So it's a real pleasure to be speaking here in front of a very special crowd, coaches from all parts of the world, very important for me because during my career, obviously my main goal, my main priority is and has been and still is and will be to become the best tennis player I can be and I'm actually in a very good moment myself. I'm in the top eight for the first time in my life and I think improving and hopefully going for more. But it's also been to a huge goal for me has been to promote wheelchair tennis. So speaking here, in front of you guys is a really good opportunity to spread key messages and to also analyze together where and how the future of wheelchair tennis should be. So I'm gonna start by through this slide celebrating that we're we are living pivotal moments in in my sport in wheelchair tennis. Paris 2024, the Paralympic Games, we live something really spectacular. 98% of the tickets those 10 days at Roland Garros were sold, which for us is really really good news. But also I lived something which you might think I'm crazy. Maybe I'm a little bit I probably am, but which for me was super positive and that is I was booed. I was booed at by the crowd.

For us, it's not very normal and I celebrate this. So we played against the French. My partner and I, Martin and I, we played against the French for the bronze medal in doubles. We went into a Suzanne Lenglin, a hundred percent of the tickets were sold. It was completely packed and when they shouted our names, Danny Kowalski, Martino La Puente from Spain, and we went in. People started booing at us like crazy and it's tense. It was really tense. But then we stopped for a moment and said, hey, man, this is what we wanted. We want people to look at us like tennis player as tennis players. We don't care. We don't give a damn about their wheelchair that they're in a wheelchair. We're going for them and that's why these moments, these type of moments that we lived in Paris, this was really good news for our sport. The feeling that not only that we're filling crowds, but that we're being respected, truly respected and seen as athletes. Over there in that picture, you can see the queen. That's the one on the left is the queen. The one on the right is the minister of sport. They were cheering like crazy. They were there the whole week. It was really it was really important for me as obviously as a tennis player, but for the sport, I think. And we are living very good moments, a lot of good news, which I'm going to speak about during today's presentation. And in general, in Paralympic sports, my first Paralympic games were London 2012.
